title: The Clock of the Cape Route
premise: In the winter of 1917, at a fog-bound colonial port on the Cape Route, Jonah Nystrom serves as a battlefield nurse in a hospital that official reports pretend does not exist, keeping a secret ledger of the wounded and dead whose names officers strike from the record. When the season's storms close the bridge — the only road out — and a troopship is announced as the last vessel to sail before spring, the garrison's hidden truths begin to surface: the ledger, an officer's forged casualty lists, and a love Jonah has kept quiet against every rule of duty. As the morning tide approaches with only one berth left on the ship, Jonah must decide whether to spend it on a wounded brother-in-arms, the officer who has become their unlikely ally and lover, or a stranger's child whose name exists only in the ledger. In the end Jonah gives the berth away, stays behind through the closed season, and chooses to make the invisible names visible — burning neither the ledger nor the chance at love, but carrying both into a spring that may never come.
about_author: Bram Pemberton is the pen name of a former merchant-marine archivist who spent a decade cataloguing port ledgers along the old colonial shipping routes. Their fiction draws on recovered hospital registers and letters found sealed in harbor-customs crates.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Jonah Nystrom's POV. In the fever ward of a port hospital the war officially ignores, Jonah records the names officers omit from dispatches, hiding the ledger beneath a loose floorboard. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: memory as an act of resistance no one has yet noticed.

chapters.title: Fog on the Cape Route
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The port settles into winter; supply ships grow scarce and rumors spread of an early closing of the causeway bridge. Jonah measures the ward's world in what can be carried — morphine vials, a photograph, thirty-one names. The beat is mounting unease beneath routine.

chapters.title: Major Aldous Vane's Clean Books
chapters.summary: Major Vane's POV. The garrison's commanding officer reviews casualty returns, striking names to protect his promotion prospects, and orders the hospital's 'irregular' records destroyed before inspection. The beat is cold bureaucratic corruption, shown from inside the machinery Jonah resists.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Storms take out the causeway; the road home shuts for the season, trapping staff, wounded, and secrets alike. A young soldier named Tam Oduya arrives with a wound no one will log. The beat is claustrophobia — invisibility was a choice until now.

chapters.title: Sister Maren's Warning
chapters.summary: Head nurse Maren's POV. Maren, who has survived three postings by knowing when to look away, warns Jonah that Vane intends to burn the irregular files and that anyone keeping them will be charged. The beat is fear offered as friendship, and the first crack in Jonah's solitude.

chapters.title: Lieutenant Ashcombe, Off Duty
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Lieutenant Elias Ashcombe, Vane's adjutant and the man Jonah has loved in silence for a year, discovers the ledger by accident — and says nothing. A stolen hour on the seawall. The beat is tenderness sharpened by danger: love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: Thirty-Two Names
chapters.summary: Tam Oduya's POV. Recovering in the ward, Tam reads the ledger and finds his own name entered where the army wrote 'unknown.' He begins helping Jonah verify entries against the men's own accounts. The beat is dignity reclaimed, one name at a time.

chapters.title: The Inspection
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. An inspector arrives ahead of schedule; Vane produces immaculate books while the real ledger sits under floorboards feet away. Jonah watches the lie performed. The beat is vertigo — how easily power rewrites the dead.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. With the bridge shut and rations short, Jonah inventories the ward: what to keep, what to abandon, whom to prioritize if evacuation comes. Maren notices the arithmetic and understands its shape. The beat is dread disguised as practicality.

chapters.title: Ashcombe's Choice
chapters.summary: Ashcombe's POV. Ordered to certify the falsified returns, Ashcombe hesitates — then quietly alters one figure to protect a wounded man's pension claim, his first small treason. The beat is conscience waking inside the machine.

chapters.title: The Ship on the Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Word arrives: a troopship will sail on the first clear tide, last departure before spring, berths for forty. Vane controls the list. Every hidden thing in the port now orbits a single piece of paper. The beat is hope curdling into competition.

chapters.title: Vane's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane drafts the berth list to bury evidence: witnesses to the falsified returns are assigned to stay behind. He tells himself it is strategy, not murder by weather. The beat is self-deception at the summit of power.

chapters.title: Maren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren offers Vane her silence about his private smuggling in exchange for berths for her sickest patients — and learns he already knows about Jonah's ledger. The beat is the sickening discovery that protection has a price and a deadline.

chapters.title: Floorboards and Fire
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Vane orders the ward searched. Jonah moves the ledger into the one place no one looks — sewn into a dead soldier's effects awaiting shipment — while Ashcombe misdirects the search party. The beat is terror braided with trust.

chapters.title: One Berth
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The final list leaves exactly one unassigned berth, and Vane makes it explicit: it is Jonah's, contingent on surrendering the ledger and forgetting the names. The beat is the novel's moral hinge compressed into a single offer.

chapters.title: Tam's Name, Spoken Aloud
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam asks Jonah not to trade the ledger for him — he'd rather stay a name than become a bargain. The ward quietly takes sides. The beat is grief and grace: the invisible choosing visibility even at cost.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Tide
chapters.summary: Ashcombe's POV. Ashcombe confronts Vane over the doctored returns, offering his own career as collateral; Vane counters by threatening to expose Ashcombe and Jonah both. The beat is love and duty colliding in a lamplit office, neither willing to yield.

chapters.title: Which Family Gets the Last Berth
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Dawn nears. Jonah weighs brother, lover, stranger's child, and the ledger itself — the family the war built versus the family denied. The beat is the novel's climax of decision, rendered in the space between heartbeats.

chapters.title: The Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. Jonah gives the berth to Tam and hands the ledger to Ashcombe, who boards as its courier, promising to publish the names ashore. They part on the quay with duty finally aligned instead of opposed. The beat is sacrifice transformed into purpose.

chapters.title: Winter Without a Bridge
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The port endures the closed season: shortages, Vane's tightening grip, and Jonah openly keeping a second ledger now that hiding is pointless. Maren stands beside them. The beat is bleak courage — visibility chosen, consequences accepted.

chapters.title: The Names Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Spring brings the first ship and Ashcombe returns with printed copies of the ledger; the names are read aloud on the quay over Vane's furious objections as the inspector's inquiry opens. The beat is vindication that costs everything and heals some things.

chapters.title: What the Clock Keeps
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, coda. On the reopened bridge, Jonah keeps the original ledger — not as accusation but as inheritance — and writes the first new name freely: their own. The beat is resolution: memory preserved, love chosen, power answered by witness.
